scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether disagreeing with HR in this situation is right or wrong. Let me start by understanding the scenario. I'm a 7-month newly hired employee at a big corporation. Last night, HR sent out a five-page memo titled "Office Discipline." They reminded everyone about various office rules, like not loitering during office hours, sticking to lunch schedules, dress code, and wearing IDs at all times. Now, in my 6 months here, HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. The company is big, with an entire floor dedicated to HR, unlike multiple departments sharing one floor. Despite their size, they're slow. It took them about 5 months to process my payroll, so the delay in ID cards isn't a surprise. Everyone without an office ID started using government-issued IDs to enter the building. This morning, security announced that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. I called HR to ask about the status of my and my colleagues' IDs. They said they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swamped with other "projects" and suggested we print our own IDs using a template they provided. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we shouldn't have to make up for HR's shortcomings by spending our own money to print IDs, especially since it should have been provided to us in the first place. We decided to keep using whatever IDs we have right now, regardless of what happens next week. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong to disagree with HR in this situation? First, I need to consider the company's policies and the role of HR. HR is responsible for issuing IDs, and their delay in providing them is a failure on their part. By suggesting that employees print their own IDs, HR is essentially shifting their responsibility onto the employees, which is unfair. Employees should not have to bear the cost or effort of something that is HR's responsibility. It's not reasonable to expect employees to print their own IDs, especially if the company has the resources to do it themselves. This could set a bad precedent where employees are expected to cover for HR's inefficiencies. Moreover, the security policy about reporting employees without IDs adds pressure on the employees. It's HR's fault for not issuing the IDs on time, and now employees are being penalized for something they can't control. This could lead to a hostile work environment and lower employee morale. Disagreeing with HR in this case seems justified because HR is not fulfilling their duties, and employees are being unfairly burdened. It's important for employees to stand up for their rights and ensure that HR takes responsibility for their tasks. However, I should also consider the potential consequences of disagreeing with HR. HR plays a crucial role in the company, handling employee relations, benefits, and policies. Disagreeing openly could lead to tension or even negative repercussions for the employees involved. But in this case, the employees are not just disagreeing; they're also taking a stand by continuing to use their own IDs despite the threat of being reported. This shows that they're not willing to compromise their rights and are asserting their position. In conclusion, while disagreeing with HR can have its risks, in this situation, it seems justified because HR is failing in their responsibilities, and employees are being unfairly treated. It's important for employees to advocate for themselves and ensure that HR fulfills their duties properly.
